newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's IG Metall discusses 1997 pay strategy.
newsitem.headline: Germany's IG Metall discusses 1997 pay strategy.

text.p: The management board of Germany's largest union, the powerful IG Metall, met on Tuesday to discuss its strategy for 1997 pay talks amid a raging dispute with employers over plans to cut sick pay.
The union reached an uneasy truce with the employers' association on Monday over the sick pay issue.

The employers backed down from an original call for companies to implement a cut in sick pay to 80 percent of normal pay from 100 percent currently in return for a pledge from IG Metall that it will suspend damaging walk-outs.
Klaus Zwickel, head of the union, said as he entered the meeting that the board would make a firm demand for the 1997 wage round after the meeting today, despite the controversy of the pay issue.
"We will be making concrete recommendations," he said.
IG Metall's current pay contract, which expires at the end of this year, awarded workers a 3.4 percent pay increase from May 1995 and a further 3.6 percent rise from November 1995.

The deal was hailed as a huge victory for the unions, coming in far higher than most employers had expected. Economists, who blame high wage rises in 1995 for a downturn in the German economy in late 1995, criticised the agreement.
The sick pay issue, aimed at helping companies to become more competitive by reining in costs, was expected to be high on IG Metall's agenda for the meeting.

Dagmar Opoczynski, spokeswoman for the union, said before the talks began that Zwickel would open the meeting by giving the board a detailed report on Monday's talks with the employers' association aimed at resolving the sick pay dispute.
"He will inform the board about yesterday's talks," she said.

German firms, hurrying to implement a new law allowing them to reduce sick pay, were shocked last week by the strength of wave of protest at their announcements that they planned to cut sick pay without union consultation.
Several companies reversed this decision on Monday pending further guidance from the employer association.
The two sides will meet again on Thursday for further talks on how to break the deadlock over the sick pay issue.
